extraction.name: ChartQA
extraction.description: A large-scale benchmark for question answering about real-world charts requiring visual and logical reasoning. It contains 20,882 charts curated from four online sources, 9,608 human-written question-answer pairs (ChartQA-H), and 23,111 machine-generated question-answer pairs derived from human-written chart summaries (ChartQA-M). The benchmark includes bar, line, and pie charts and open-vocabulary answers.
extraction.creator: Ahmed Masry, Do Xuan Long, Jia Qing Tan, Shafiq Joty, Enamul Hoque
extraction.citeAs: Ahmed Masry, Do Xuan Long, Jia Qing Tan, Shafiq Joty, and Enamul Hoque. 2022. ChartQA: A Benchmark for Question Answering about Charts with Visual and Logical Reasoning. arXiv:2203.10244v1, 19 March 2022.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Charts were crawled from Statista, Pew Research, Our World in Data (OWID), and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) to cover varied topics and visual styles. Only chart images were crawled from Pew because underlying data tables were unavailable. For the other sources, the authors extracted underlying data tables, metadata such as title and chart type, SVG files, and associated text descriptions. Bounding boxes of chart elements were extracted from SVG files to train data extraction models. Human-authored question-answer pairs were collected through Amazon Mechanical Turk, and additional pairs were generated from Statista's human-written summaries. Only publicly available charts complying with source terms and conditions were used.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Underlying data tables were not available for the Pew charts, so only chart images were crawled from that source.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Publicly available chart images from statista.com, pewresearch.org, ourworldindata.org, and oecd.org. Statista, OWID, and OECD additionally supplied underlying data tables, chart metadata, SVG files, and associated text descriptions. Statista's human-written chart summaries supplied the source text for machine-generated question-answer pairs.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset was augmented with 23,111 question-answer pairs generated from Statista's human-written summaries using two pretrained T5 models fine-tuned on SQuAD: one for answer extraction and one for answer-aware question generation. Human-written and machine-generated question-answer pairs were randomly divided into training, validation, and test sets. ChartQA-H contains 7,398 training, 960 validation, and 1,250 test questions; ChartQA-M contains 20,901 training, 960 validation, and 1,250 test questions.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Generated questions were filtered out when their answers could not be found in the underlying chart data table. The machine-generated test set was manually cleaned by removing invalid questions. Chart-element bounding boxes were extracted from SVG files. For experiments without supplied data tables, an extended ChartOCR pipeline detected chart marks and textual elements, read text using CRAFT, estimated data values, and associated values with axis and legend labels using color, proximity, and alignment.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Amazon Mechanical Turk workers were asked to create two question-answer pairs per chart, focusing on compositional questions involving at least two mathematical or logical operations and visual questions referring to attributes such as color, height, and length. Another annotator answered the same questions. Each HIT involved verifying two previously asked questions and providing two new pairs. Workers were selected using a 95% acceptance-rate criterion, 5,000 completed HITs, and a qualification pretest. Chart data labels were displayed so workers could perform calculations accurately. Workers received $0.60 per task, with an estimated task duration of 3–5 minutes, and annotations were anonymized. Machine-generated pairs were produced by T5 answer-extraction and answer-aware question-generation models fine-tuned on SQuAD and applied to Statista summaries.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human answers were accepted as correct when the original worker's answer and the verifying annotator's answer exactly matched; disagreements were manually checked to select the final correct answer. Exact-match agreement was 61.04%. Manual analysis of 500 random samples found 78.55% agreement when accounting for typos and lexical variations. After heuristic filtering, manual analysis of 1,250 machine-generated pairs found 86.64% complete, answerable, and correct given the chart. Invalid machine-generated test questions were manually removed.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Each human-annotated chart received two question-answer pairs. Each human-authored question was answered by two workers: its author and a second annotator. Disagreements received additional manual checking.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: T5 models fine-tuned on SQuAD for answer extraction and answer-aware question generation; extended ChartOCR and CRAFT for automatic chart data extraction.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Chart content includes aggregate demographic and social information, including gender, age groups, poverty, geography, and public opinion. Examples include questions about men's opinions, comparisons between age groups, poverty percentages, and national populations. All crowdworker annotations were anonymized to protect annotator privacy; the paper does not specify personal attributes collected about annotators.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark is intended to support systems that answer users' questions about charts, reducing the perceptual and cognitive effort required for chart analysis. The authors warn that their models could be abused to mislead the public about chart content and implications and that model outputs are not guaranteed to be correct. Ethical considerations included respecting source intellectual property and usage conditions, compensating annotators with reference to the US minimum wage of $7.25 per hour, and anonymizing annotations.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Bar charts are the most common chart type across the sources, while pie charts are less common. Topic distributions vary by source: 45.4% of Pew charts concern U.S. Politics & Policy, while Society is the most frequent topic for OECD (34.0%) and OWID (26.0%). Human annotation deliberately emphasizes compositional and visual reasoning questions; 76.33% of 300 sampled human-written questions were compositional or both visual and compositional.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Machine-generated questions can be incomplete or unanswerable from the chart because of the mismatch between SQuAD training data and chart-summary inputs. Heuristic filtering does not eliminate all invalid pairs: 86.64% of 1,250 manually inspected pairs were complete, answerable, and correct. Human-written questions can contain informal language and typos. The dataset contains three chart types: bar, line, and pie. Pew charts lack supplied underlying data tables. Automatic table extraction remains error-prone for diverse real-world chart styles, with reported ChartQA extraction accuracy of 83.85%; the extraction evaluation metric does not account for extracted textual tokens, which are particularly noisy in real-world figures.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, testing, and fine-tuning of chart question-answering models requiring visual and logical reasoning with open-vocabulary answers. The paper evaluates settings with supplied underlying data tables and with tables automatically extracted from chart images, and investigates transfer learning from PlotQA to ChartQA. Numeric answers are evaluated with a tolerance of 5% of the gold answer; nonnumeric answers require exact matches. Source usage conditions described in the paper include academic use of publicly available Statista charts, Pew attribution requirements, OECD use subject to applicable restrictions, and open-access use of OWID data.
